Causal effect of a treatment on latent class membership

intervene_membership.Rd

Estimates \(\Delta_k = P(C(1) = k) - P(C(0) = k)\), the effect of a binary treatment on the probability of belonging to each latent class \(k\), using a measurement model fitted with latentmixtures::lca() or latentmixtures::lpa() without covariates on the same rows. The default estimator is augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) with bias-corrected (BCH) pseudo-outcomes and 5-fold cross-fitting: doubly robust with respect to the propensity model and the latent class regression, provided the measurement model is invariant across the treatment and the confounders. Standard errors come from the influence function and include the uncertainty of the measurement model.

Usage

intervene_membership(
  model,
  data,
  treatment,
  confounders = NULL,
  estimator = "aipw",
  propensity_model = "linear",
  outcome_model = "linear",
  folds = 5,
  trim = 0,
  seed = 1,
  learners = NULL,
  bound = 0.01
)

Arguments

model

A latentmix model (LCA or LPA without covariates), fitted to the same rows as data.

data

A data frame with the same rows as the data model was fitted to (or, in the positional form, the treatment vector).

treatment

The binary treatment: a column of data (tidyselect; numeric 0/1, logical or a two-level factor, whose second level is "treated"), or a 0/1 vector (in the positional form, the confounder matrix).

confounders

Confounders: columns of data (tidyselect, e.g. c(age, female) or starts_with("x")), or a numeric matrix / data frame, or NULL. Factors and character columns are dummy-coded.

estimator

"aipw" (default), "ipw_bch", "or", "ipw_modal", "aipw_posterior" or "naive" (see Details).

propensity_model, outcome_model

Working models for the propensity score (logistic regression) and the latent class regression: "linear" (main effects) or "quadratic" (adds squares, pairwise products and treatment-by-covariate terms). Machine-learning learners are also accepted (see learners).

folds

Number of cross-fitting folds (1 = no cross-fitting).

trim

Truncate estimated propensity scores to [trim, 1 - trim] (0 = no truncation).

seed

Random seed for the fold assignment.

learners

Machine-learning nuisance models. Besides "linear" and "quadratic", propensity_model and outcome_model accept a learner fitted within the cross-fitting training folds: "lasso", "lasso_quadratic", "elasticnet", "ridge" (penalised GLMs with cross-validated \(\lambda\)), "forest" (random forest), "boost" (gradient-boosted trees; needs the Julia package EvoTrees.jl) or "superlearner" (stacked ensemble). With a learner, the class regression estimates \(P(\hat c = j \mid A = a, X)\) in each arm and maps it through \(D^{-1}\). learners is the library of the "superlearner": a character vector of names ("mean", "glm", "glm_quadratic", "lasso", "lasso_quadratic", "elasticnet", "ridge", "forest", "boost"), or NULL for the default library (mean, glm, lasso, lasso_quadratic, forest).

bound

With a learner, propensity scores are bounded to [bound, 1 - bound] (forests can predict 0 or 1). Not applied to "linear" / "quadratic".

Value

An object of class lcc_result, a list with

estimator, K, n, folds

estimator, number of classes, rows used, folds;

delta

the effects \(\Delta_k\) (length K, summing to zero);

se, se_fixed

their standard errors including / excluding the measurement model uncertainty;

psi1, psi0, se_psi1, se_psi0

potential-outcome class probabilities \(P(C(1) = k)\), \(P(C(0) = k)\) and their standard errors;

propensity_range, pseudo_range

ranges of the estimated propensity scores and of the pseudo-outcomes (diagnostics);

entropy

entropy of the measurement model;

treatment, confounders

variable names;

propensity_model, outcome_model, trim, call

the settings;

propensity

data frame of the cross-fitted (and trimmed) propensity scores of the analysed rows: row (row of data), treatment and ps, used by autoplot() (type = "overlap");

text

Julia's printed summary.

Methods: print(), tidy(), glance(), as.data.frame(), coef(), nobs(), causal_table() and lm_table().

Details

Method. Let \(\hat c(Y)\) be the modal class of the fitted measurement model and \(D_{kj} = P(\hat c = j \mid C = k)\) its classification-error matrix (latentmixtures::classification_table()). The BCH pseudo-outcome \(Z_k = (D^{-1})[\hat c(Y), k]\) (Bolck, Croon & Hagenaars 2004; Vermunt 2010) is an unbiased proxy of the class indicator: \(E[Z_k \mid A, X] = P(C = k \mid A, X)\) when the measurement model is invariant. The AIPW estimator (Bang & Robins 2005) of \(\psi_k(1) = P(C(1) = k)\) is $$\hat\psi_k(1) = P_n\{\tilde\mu_k(1, X) + A(Z_k - \tilde\mu_k(1, X))/\tilde e(X)\},$$ with working models \(\tilde e\) for the propensity score and \(\tilde\mu_k\) for the latent class regression, fitted by cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al. 2018); likewise for \(a = 0\). It is consistent if either working model is correct. Earlier approaches weight a one-step latent class model by the inverse propensity score (Lanza, Coffman & Xu 2013) or combine IPW with the bias-adjusted three-step method (Clouth et al. 2022); "aipw" adds the outcome-regression augmentation and cross-fitting.

Estimators.

  • "aipw": AIPW with BCH pseudo-outcomes (default; doubly robust).

  • "ipw_bch": inverse probability weighting of the BCH pseudo-outcomes (consistent if the propensity model is correct; cf. Clouth et al. 2022).

  • "or": outcome regression (g-computation) with the latent class regression estimated by three-step ML (Vermunt 2010; consistent if that regression is correct).

  • "ipw_modal", "aipw_posterior", "naive": comparison estimators that use the modal class or the posterior probabilities as if they were the true class (IPW with the modal class, AIPW with posterior probabilities, unadjusted difference of modal class shares). They ignore classification error and are biased in general.

Assumptions. Consistency, positivity (\(0 < e(x) < 1\)), no unmeasured confounding of the treatment given the confounders, and a measurement model that holds and is invariant with respect to the treatment and the confounders (no differential item functioning: \(Y \perp (A, X) \mid C\)), with an invertible classification-error matrix. Double robustness covers the propensity and class regression models, not the measurement model: under DIF the estimator is biased whatever the working models. Check overlap with glance() (propensity range) and consider trim.

Standard errors. The default (se in tidy.lcc_result(): "robust") stacks the estimating equations of the measurement model, the classification-error matrix and the effect, so it includes the uncertainty from the first step; "fixed" treats the measurement model as known and shows how much that step contributes.

Calling forms. Three forms are accepted:

  • data first (tidy): intervene_membership(model, data, treatment = a, confounders = c(x1, x2)), where treatment and confounders are tidyselect expressions on data. The data frame may also come first, data |> intervene_membership(model, treatment = a, ...).

  • vectors: intervene_membership(model, treatment = a, confounders = X) with a 0/1 vector and a numeric matrix / data frame.

  • positional: intervene_membership(model, A, X).

Row alignment and missing data. In every form the rows must be those of the data the model was fitted to, in the same order (nrow == model$ninput); this is checked for the number of rows only. Treatment and confounders must be observed on every row the model analysed. Factors and character confounders are dummy-coded (first level as reference).

How to use

  1. Fit the measurement model to the outcome indicators only, without covariates (m <- latentmixtures::lca(data, items, K = 3)), choose K and check latentmixtures::convergence(m).

  2. Call intervene_membership(m, data, treatment = ..., confounders = c(...)) with the data frame the model was fitted to (same rows, same order). The treatment may be 0/1, logical or a two-level factor; factor confounders are dummy-coded.

  3. Read \(\Delta_k\) and its standard error in the printout; tidy() gives a table and autoplot(r, type = "overlap") the propensity overlap.

  4. Check the nuisance models: propensity_model = "quadratic", outcome_model = "quadratic", a learner, trim = 0.01, or estimator = "ipw_bch".

  5. Probe what the data cannot check: intervene_membership_sensitivity() (unmeasured confounding) and intervene_dif() (non-invariant measurement); for heterogeneity, intervene_subgroup(). See vignette("function-guide").

References

Bang, H., & Robins, J. M. (2005). Doubly robust estimation in missing data and causal inference models. Biometrics, 61(4), 962–973. doi:10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00377.x

Bolck, A., Croon, M., & Hagenaars, J. (2004). Estimating latent structure models with categorical variables: One-step versus three-step estimators. Political Analysis, 12(1), 3–27. doi:10.1093/pan/mph001

Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W., & Robins, J. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal, 21(1), C1–C68. doi:10.1111/ectj.12097

Clouth, F. J., Pauws, S., Mols, F., & Vermunt, J. K. (2022). A new three-step method for using inverse propensity weighting with latent class analysis. Advances in Data Analysis and Classification, 16(2), 351–371. doi:10.1007/s11634-021-00456-5

Lanza, S. T., Coffman, D. L., & Xu, S. (2013). Causal inference in latent class analysis. Structural Equation Modeling, 20(3), 361–383. doi:10.1080/10705511.2013.797816

Vermunt, J. K. (2010). Latent class modeling with covariates: Two improved three-step approaches. Political Analysis, 18(4), 450–469. doi:10.1093/pan/mpq025

See also

intervene_effect() for interventions on the indicators themselves; tidy.lcc_result(), causal_table(); vignette("latentclasscausal").

Examples

data(programme)
# \donttest{
# Question: does the school programme (programme, 0/1) move students between latent
# wellbeing classes six months later, adjusting for baseline confounders?
# 1. measurement model of the eight follow-up items only (no treatment, no covariates)
m <- latentmixtures::lca(programme, low_mood:friends, K = 3)
#> Starting Julia ...
latentmixtures::convergence(m)          # best LL replicated: a stable 3-class solution
#> Convergence check: ✓ no problems found
#>   best start converged      yes (240 EM iterations)
#>   stage-2 starts converged  20 / 20
#>   best LL replicated        20 times
#>   LL at EM / after Newton   -7785.7692 / -7785.7692 (gain 3.0e-06; max |gradient| 3.2e-12)
#>   smallest class            0.204
round(sapply(latentmixtures::itemprobs(m), function(p) p["1", ]), 2)
#>        low_mood worry sleep lonely hopeless enjoy confident friends
#> class1     0.05  0.13  0.10   0.04     0.02  0.97      0.91    0.90
#> class2     0.30  0.44  0.30   0.33     0.10  0.64      0.51    0.72
#> class3     0.86  0.83  0.68   0.68     0.55  0.25      0.15    0.39
# classes: 1 Flourishing (enjoy 0.97), 2 Moderate, 3 Distressed (low_mood 0.86)
# 2. the causal effect (AIPW, BCH pseudo-outcomes, 5-fold cross-fitting)
r <- intervene_membership(m, programme, treatment = programme,
                          confounders = c(female, age, low_ses, distress, belonging))
r
#> ▸ Causal effect of a treatment on latent class membership
#>   AIPW, BCH pseudo-outcomes, 5-fold cross-fitting; N = 2000, K = 3
#>   Treatment:    programme
#>   Confounders:  female, age, low_ses, distress, belonging
#> 
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>            P(C¹=k)  P(C⁰=k)       Δ     SE            95% CI      p
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>   Class 1    0.623    0.429   0.194  0.031    [0.134, 0.254]  <.001
#>   Class 2    0.242    0.294  −0.052  0.037   [−0.123, 0.020]   .160
#>   Class 3    0.135    0.277  −0.143  0.021  [−0.185, −0.101]  <.001
#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#>   Δ = P(C¹=k) − P(C⁰=k); SE from the influence function incl. the measurement model.
#>   Diagnostics: entropy = 0.666, propensity range [0.022, 0.922]
# Delta = +0.196 (95\% CI 0.136 to 0.256) for Flourishing: participation raises its share
# from 43.0\% to 62.6\%; Distressed falls from 27.7\% to 13.6\% (Delta = -0.141).
# True effects: +0.179, -0.059, -0.120. Entropy 0.666, propensities in [0.019, 0.923].
tidy(r)    # one row per class, for tables
#>      term class    estimate  std.error statistic      p.value   conf.low
#> 1 Class 1     1  0.19412038 0.03079076  6.304501 2.891241e-10  0.1337716
#> 2 Class 2     2 -0.05151209 0.03663291 -1.406170 1.596737e-01 -0.1233113
#> 3 Class 3     3 -0.14260828 0.02144657 -6.649467 2.941555e-11 -0.1846428
#>     conf.high      psi1 psi1.std.error      psi0 psi0.std.error
#> 1  0.25446916 0.6231211     0.04064258 0.4290007     0.03583616
#> 2  0.02028709 0.2420179     0.03667034 0.2935300     0.03076214
#> 3 -0.10057377 0.1348610     0.01684969 0.2774693     0.02435104
# 3. checks: the naive difference is near zero (confounding by indication); flexible
#    nuisance models give the same answer (+0.195, -0.054, -0.141)
intervene_membership(m, programme, treatment = programme,
                     confounders = c(female, age, low_ses, distress, belonging),
                     estimator = "naive")$delta
#> [1]  0.022414306 -0.019912819 -0.002501486
intervene_membership(m, programme, treatment = programme,
                     confounders = c(female, age, low_ses, distress, belonging),
                     propensity_model = "quadratic", outcome_model = "quadratic", trim = 0.01)
#> ▸ Causal effect of a treatment on latent class membership
#>   AIPW, BCH pseudo-outcomes, 5-fold cross-fitting; N = 2000, K = 3

#>   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

#>   Class 2    0.234    0.304  −0.070  0.038   [−0.144, 0.004]   .063
